doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Collective improvisation, swing dancing's return and 1950s campus bands
summary: He says schools neglect small-band work, notes college swing dancing and informal 1950s campus bands.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: think enough time is spent on collective improvisation, small band work. The real world, let’s face it, is not going to be a big band reading those parts. And I do not like a lot of the solos put out by great technicians, I just feel that they’ve learned things almost by rote, by too much Arban book and not enough simple stuff. All the things I’ve been talking about. My whole philosophy I think a lot of it is lacking in the music school. We didn’t have that much in music schools, because we did it by playing. Of course jazz was the music of the time you know and so I think these are substitutes now, you’ve got to create a lab band, you’ve got to create a big band, you’ve got to take one course and they divide you up into six small group improvisation things and you try to pick the best guys to work together and you’re creating the, you have to create the situations that happened automatically when I was in school. I was fortunate enough to play every weekend at a party where people were loving it, you know, playing our music. I think it’s coming back with swing dancing, I think younger people are getting interested much more so. My son is out in Michigan, has already got three or four clubs in Ann Arbor where they have jazz. I stopped at one place and I saw him sit in one night. I mean and he’s just starting and they encouraged him. So there are natural settings for this music and I do think the involvement of young people in dancing can turn a corner unless they just make it a fad and just say this is retro. If the Squirrel Nut Zippers and their leader, from what I read about him he’s genuine and if they are not going to be a typical retro band maybe they will set a standard. But I do see young people, I played a club in Westchester, a new jazz club, The August Lounge, out there were college aged kids learning how to they call it swing dancing, it’s jitterbugging, I mean tossing each other over the shoulder, practicing right on the dance floor. I played a job at Columbia University — boy I’m talking too much here — last year with a fraternity party where the kids were lined up. They were charging admission for kids from other fraternities for kids to come for their annual swing dance. There must have been 300 people in this fraternity house, on 110th Street in New York City. Swing dancing. It was wonderful. So maybe there will — I don’t know I guess I hedged a little bit because I really don’t want to start attacking what’s going on in schools but I do think if some of the things that I was talking about were covered, kids would, young people — I hate the word kids — young people would be aware of what the real world is. And maybe the teachers, some of them are not quite up to the task of for instance collective improvisation. If a teacher’s tastes are bebop and a kid come here with a more traditional thing, who’s going to say what? You’re improvising wrong? What are you going to do? It was like before Little League baseball we went up and played baseball in the hayfields in Prospect Park, New Jersey. That’s where we learned as kids. It wasn’t all so organized. So maybe with the swing dancing kids will be, there will be informal groups forming on campuses. That’s the way it was in the 50s. Every college © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-

campus in the eastern seaboard had two or three jazz bands. Some of them were swing, some of them were bebop, some of them were Dixieland. At the Colgate Winter Carnival they’d have a full day Saturday from 10 in the morning until 5 at night, 5 in the evening, one jazz band after another. A solid day of jazz in the auditorium there. All informal groups. Nothing, no auspices. Colleges have had to do it this other way because it’s not been, jazz has not been central to the peers and they’re not that interested in it so a kid is going to gravitate to play rock or whatever.
Well, and a lot of the players I work with are too.
